Lower Bound of Sorting
Sorting algorithms were based on comparisons.
W.l.o.g all values distinct. Only ordinal position of value matters.
Given input (@,,@2,...,A,), the sorting problem is to find a
permutation zr of {1,2, ...,n}s.t. An(1) < Aggy < + < Ann).
Comparison sorting is modeled
by a full binary decision tree.

Every leaf of a decision tree is a permutation (x(1), (2), «, m(n)).
Execution of sorting algorithm on given input corresponds to a root-
to-leaf path yielding the sorted input aq7(4) < Agq(z) < +++ < Aan).
Because correct algorithm must be able to produce any permutation
of the input, each of n! permutations must present at distinct leaf.
Consequently, the decision tree must have at least n! leaves.

Theorem: (M. Ben-Or) Any comparison sorting algorithm requires
Q(n log n) comparisons in the worst case.

path) having l leaves. The tree is full binary hence 1 < 2”.

Quicksort (C.A.R. Hoare 1962)
Divide-and-conquer algorithm comprising three steps. Given A[p..7],
* Divide: Partition A[p..r] into Alp..q —1], Alq], Alq +1..r] s.t.
Alp..q — 1] < Al[q] and A[q] < A[q + 1..r].
* Conquer: Sort A[p..q — 1] and Alq + 1..1r] recursively.
* Combine: No work required since A[p..7] is already sorted.

pivot q € [p..r] choice.
Leftward shift of elements < pivot x = A[r] and proper reposition of
pivot next to them ensures that > elements are rightward.
